A client under test must derive its lifecycle from the protocol version it is told to run — stateful (initialize handshake) for dated versions through 2025-11-25, stateless (per-request _meta) for the 2026 draft — and use the forwarded MCP_CONFORMANCE_PROTOCOL_VERSION.

Request metadata (client): send MCP-Protocol-Version on every POST, populate the three required _meta fields on every request, keep the header equal to _meta.protocolVersion, and retry with a supported version when the first is rejected.

Let the Client negotiate the protocol version (it probes the server and falls back to the classic handshake for older servers) rather than pinning a version, unless you have a specific reason to control it.

Use the sdk subcommand as the cross-SDK inner loop (it clones, builds, and runs the local conformance build against a ref) and pass --mode client or --mode server, since each side is tested and scored independently.

Model an SDK's example conformance server on the reference everything-server: implement the full feature surface (tools, resources, prompts, all log levels, completion, list-changed, subscribe/update), use the standardized names (test_ prefix for tools/prompts, test:// for resources), and reproduce its automatic behaviors (dynamic registration about 2s after start, watched-resource update about every 3s) so one suite verifies every SDK.
Assess an SDK's tier with the tier-check subcommand against SEP-1730.

Every check should carry specReferences to the governing spec section, and its severity must follow the spec keyword — MUST/MUST NOT to FAILURE, SHOULD/SHOULD NOT to WARNING — noting CI treats WARNING as failing, so Tier-1 SDKs must satisfy SHOULDs too.

Read the traceability manifest correctly: it is generated from a real reference-SDK run (so dynamic check IDs resolve), tested means the check ID was emitted (not that any SDK passes — that is tier-check), and a SEP absent from it has no conformance artifacts and is not-started.
Relegation (SEP-1730): an SDK drops from Tier 1 to Tier 2 if any conformance test fails continuously for 4 weeks, and from Tier 2 to Tier 3 if more than 20% fail continuously for 4 weeks.
Take a SEP's requirement levels from its spec diff (the docs/specification/draft/ change), not the SEP summary or PR description, since the governing keyword lives in the spec text.

Review against the spec diff as ground truth: read the RFC-2119 sentences yourself rather than trusting the PR description or SEP summary, and treat a SEP's conformance-test-case table as authoritative for its cases, flagging a table/prose mismatch as a spec gap rather than silently resolving it.

Ship every new scenario with both a passing example (extend the everything-client/server) and a negative test that asserts the specific FAILURE/WARNING, because a green run only proves no false-positive, not that the check catches anything.

Demand proof it runs and a real negative test: the PR must cite a real implementation it ran green against (the everything-server or an external SDK via the pkg.pr.new preview), and its negative test must pin the specific failing check slugs rather than merely assert the failure count is greater than zero.

Know the output contract: results land in results/<scenario>-<timestamp>/ (server mode results/server-<scenario>-<timestamp>/), and each result is a ConformanceCheck (id, name, description, status, timestamp, specReferences, details) in checks.json.

Emit a structured, timestamped aggregated report: one JSON report per server (named <server>.json under output/), an aggregate servers_validation.json, and a Markdown summary table of per-server status/errors/warnings — recording Name, Command, Status, counts, and report file, and adding an Error_Message on failures.

Import protocol types from the vendored spec-types/<version> copies (not @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) so scenarios can target draft versions before any SDK implements them, and never hand-edit those files — refresh via npm run sync-schema and let SOURCE record the commit.

Import the schema version a scenario or connection actually uses: a scenario imports the version matching its source.introducedIn, and a Connection imports the version whose lifecycle it implements (stateful to 2025-11-25, stateless to draft).

OAuth client authorization-server binding: on a Protected-Resource-Metadata flip to a new authorization server (a new issuer surfacing on a 401), the client MUST re-register with the new AS rather than reuse the old credentials.
OAuth client resource validation: per RFC 8707 a client MUST verify the PRM resource matches the server URL it is accessing and abort authorization on a mismatch.
Elicitation client: apply default values for omitted fields (string, integer, number, enum, boolean) before returning an elicitation response.

Elicitation (server): include default values in the elicitation schema across string, integer, number, enum, and boolean fields, and encode enum schemas by shape (untitled single-select as an enum array, titled single-select as oneOf with const/title, the legacy titled form as the deprecated enumNames, untitled multi-select as items.enum, titled multi-select as items.anyOf).
MCP request headers (client): on Streamable HTTP POSTs send Mcp-Method (mirroring the JSON-RPC method) and Mcp-Name (mirroring params.name or params.uri for tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get).

MCP request-header validation (server, SEP-2243): reject a request whose Mcp-Method or Mcp-Name header disagrees with the body (or is missing for a name-carrying body) with HTTP 400 and JSON-RPC -32020 (HeaderMismatch); treat header names case-insensitively but values case-sensitively, accept optional whitespace around Mcp-Name per RFC 9110 section 5.5, and reject a request where a custom header is omitted while its value is present in the body.

Select the Client transport by the type of its single positional argument: an MCPServer/Server instance for in-process, a URL string for Streamable HTTP, or a transport object (usable as `async with ... as (read, write)`) for anything else.

Multi-Round Tool Resolution (client): echo requestState unchanged on retry, include none when the server sent none, use a new JSON-RPC id per retry, treat a missing resultType as complete, and never leak inputResponses or requestState into other requests.

SSE retry (client): respect the retry field (wait the given milliseconds), treat a graceful stream closure as reconnectable (reconnect via GET), and send Last-Event-ID on reconnection for resumability.

InputRequiredResult (server): respond with InputRequiredResult (inputRequests and/or requestState) to gather input; always include resultType, never return it on unsupported methods, reject tampered requestState, include inputRequests only for declared client capabilities, and return JSON-RPC errors for protocol-level input errors.

Stateless requests (server, SEP-2575): carry the request JSON-RPC id on every error, and reject a request with missing _meta — or _meta lacking io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientInfo, or clientCapabilities — with -32602.
Concurrent SSE (server): give each POST request its own SSE stream with a unique stream ID, and keep the standalone GET stream (without Last-Event-ID) limited to one per session.

SSE polling and resumption (server): send a priming event (id plus empty data) and a retry field on POST SSE streams, and support closing a stream mid-operation then replaying events on reconnect with Last-Event-ID including via GET.
Tasks capability (SEP-2663): advertise the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension, gate the v2 task surface on capability negotiation, and support SEP-2575 per-request capability overrides.

Tasks dispatch (SEP-2663): reject the removed v1 methods tasks/result and tasks/list with -32601; allow server-directed task creation without a client task hint (tolerating and ignoring the legacy task param on sync tools); let a fast operation return a sync ToolResult; stamp every non-task response with the resultType 'complete' discriminator; and guarantee strong consistency, where tasks/get right after a CreateTaskResult resolves and an unknown taskId returns -32602.

Tasks required-capability (SEP-2575/2663): if a required-task tool is called by a client that did not declare the tasks extension at initialize, reject with -32021 (MissingRequiredClientCapability) and put a requiredCapabilities object (mirroring InitializeRequest) in the error data so the client can self-describe.

Tasks wire hygiene (SEP-2663): the tasks-v2 wire defines no requestState (keep it off CreateTaskResult and DetailedTask), uses the renamed ttlMs and pollIntervalMs fields, enforces no-early-TTL-expiry, and drops the redundant v1 related-task _meta key because the taskId is already at root.
Tier thresholds (SEP-1730): Tier 1 requires a 100% conformance pass rate, Tier 2 at least 80%, and Tier 3 no minimum, where the pass rate is passed/(passed+failed)*100 over date-versioned scenarios.

Tier definitions (SEP-1730): an issue is triaged at its first label (labeling and validity, not resolution), and a P0 is a CVSS>=7.0 security vulnerability or a core-functionality failure blocking connection, message exchange, or use of core primitives.

Tier responsiveness commitments (SEP-1730): new-feature support before each spec release (Tier 1) versus within 6 months (Tier 2); issue triage within 2 business days versus within 30 days; P0 resolution within 7 days versus within 14.

Tier release, docs, and policy obligations (SEP-1730): Tier 1 needs a stable release >=1.0.0 with no pre-release plus a documented breaking-change policy, all-feature docs with examples, a published dependency policy, and a concrete roadmap; Tier 2 needs at least one stable release, core-feature docs, a dependency policy, and a plan toward Tier 1.

Tier 1 gate — require ALL of: server and client conformance at 100% (date-versioned), triage compliance >=90% within 2 business days, all P0s resolved within 7 days, a stable release >=1.0.0 with no pre-release, a documented breaking-change policy, all non-experimental features documented with examples, a published dependency policy, and a concrete roadmap.

Tier 2 gate — require ALL of: server and client conformance >=80% (date-versioned), triage compliance >=80% within 1 month, P0s resolved within 2 weeks, at least one stable release >=1.0.0, core-feature docs, a published dependency policy, and a plan toward Tier 1; otherwise the SDK is Tier 3.

Understand the traceability YAML's job (SEP-2484): map each spec-diff normative sentence to a check: ID (testable) or an excluded: reason (not testable); the CLI scaffolds the skeleton and you fill the rows from the diff, and the SEP number is the source PR number.
When a requirement is ambiguous, leave a TODO: row rather than guess, because humans review the traceability yaml before scenarios are written.
Diff the traceability YAML against the spec sentences and flag any row that paraphrases rather than quotes, claims a keyword level the spec does not support, or asserts something the spec never says.

Map RFC 2119 severity to YAML: MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, and REQUIRED become a check: row at FAILURE; SHOULD and SHOULD NOT become a check: row at WARNING; MAY and OPTIONAL produce no row at all.

Follow traceability YAML conventions: use the same id for SUCCESS and FAILURE, lowercase-kebab slugs from the verb phrase, check: rows leading with check: (then text, then optional url), excluded: rows leading with text: (then excluded, then optional issue), and all check: rows before all excluded: rows, separated by one blank line and never interleaved.

Match the Inspector launch wrapper to how the server is distributed: `npx <pkg>` for an npm package, `uvx <pkg>` for a PyPI package, `node <entry>.js` for a local TypeScript server, and `uv --directory <path> run <pkg>` for a local Python server.

Launch the Inspector via npx without cloning its repository (Node.js ^22.7.5 required): pass server arguments directly, set the server's environment variables with -e, and separate inspector flags from server arguments with `--`.
Use the server connection pane to select the transport and, for local servers, set the command-line arguments and environment before connecting.

Connect the server end via mcpServer.connect(serverTransport) with the high-level McpServer (which delegates to this.server.connect); with the low-level Server class, call server.connect(serverTransport) directly.

Exercise each capability surface through its tab rather than only checking connectivity: Resources (metadata, content, subscriptions), Prompts (custom arguments and previewed output), and Tools (custom inputs and observed results).
Begin every Inspector session by verifying basic connectivity and confirming capability negotiation before deeper testing.

Treat the MCP Inspector as two cooperating parts — the MCPI React web UI and the MCPP Node.js protocol-bridge (an MCP client plus HTTP server spanning stdio, SSE, and streamable-http) — and do not mistake the proxy for a traffic-intercepting network proxy.
Expect the MCPI UI on port 6274 and the MCPP proxy on port 6277, and resolve port conflicts by overriding CLIENT_PORT and SERVER_PORT rather than changing code.

Keep the Inspector proxy bound to localhost (its default) because it can spawn local processes and reach any MCP server; bind to all interfaces with HOST=0.0.0.0 only inside a trusted, isolated network, and never expose the proxy to untrusted networks.
Reach for the MCP Inspector first: use it as an interactive, transport-agnostic way to invoke a server's tools, prompts, and resources and watch its notification stream before deeper debugging.

Treat Inspector timeouts (MCP_SERVER_REQUEST_TIMEOUT default 300000 ms; MCP_REQUEST_MAX_TOTAL_TIMEOUT default 60000 ms) as client-side cancels independent of server-side timeouts — whichever elapses first wins — and raise them for elicitation or long-running tools.

Drive an MCP Client entirely through `async with Client(...)`: entering the block connects and negotiates and leaving it disconnects, so never call a connect()/close() pair and never reuse a Client after its block has exited.

Design the CLI test suite for safe parallelism: run in parallel across files but sequentially within a file, make each config file unique with crypto.randomUUID(), allocate HTTP/SSE ports dynamically, depend only on built-in MCP test servers, and do not expect coverage numbers because subprocess-run code is untrackable by Vitest.
Prefer the in-memory transport session helper (create_connected_server_and_client_session) for MCP server tests instead of starting a real server or network, which yields fast, isolated tests.

Make logging load-bearing and structured: instrument initialization, resource access, tool execution, errors, and performance; use consistent formats, context, timestamps, and request IDs; log stack traces and track error patterns, recovery, timing, resource usage, message sizes, and latency.

Treat debug logging and debugging access as a security surface: sanitize logs, protect credentials, mask personal information, and enforce access control (verify permissions, check authentication, monitor access patterns).
Always use absolute paths in server configuration, .env files, and the command executable, because a client-launched stdio server's working directory may be undefined (e.g. / on macOS).
Declare a server's required environment variables explicitly via the client config's env key rather than relying on stdio env inheritance, which passes only a limited, platform-dependent subset.

Expose the connected client session to tests through an async-generator pytest fixture that opens create_connected_server_and_client_session(app, raise_exceptions=True) with `async with` and yields the session, so teardown is automatic and server-side exceptions propagate into the test.

Consider snapshot testing (inline-snapshot's snapshot(...)) to pin expected tool results; it eases test authoring and is promoted as best practice, but it is optional and adds the inline-snapshot dependency alongside pytest.

Exercise tools through the session: await client_session.call_tool(name, arguments) and assert on the returned CallToolResult, checking both its text content (the TextContent list) and its machine-readable structuredContent.

When a tool declares an output/structured schema, call client.listTools() before client.callTool() so the client caches and validates against the tool's schemas, and assert on the result's structuredContent.

Page every `list_*` call with a cursor loop: pass `cursor=`, collect the results, and stop when `next_cursor` is `None`; this loop is correct against every server even though `MCPServer` returns a single page.

Never assume a list call returns every item: listTools, listPrompts, listResources and listResourceTemplates are cursor-paginated, so loop passing the previous response's nextCursor as cursor until nextCursor is undefined.
Use the SDK's built-in ping() for peer health checks rather than a custom heartbeat: both client and server expose it and the remote responds automatically with no registered handler.

For a bounded health check set a millisecond timeout on client.ping(); remember the low-level server.server.ping() has no timeout option, so enforce your own deadline when pinging from the server side.

Wire progress reporting end-to-end for long-running requests: provide an onprogress callback on the client (the SDK auto-assigns the progressToken) and have the server emit notifications/progress via extra.sendNotification with the progressToken in params.
Guard server-side progress emission: send a progress notification only when extra._meta.progressToken is defined, i.e. only when the caller actually requested progress.

Make long-running calls cancellable: the client passes an AbortSignal ({ signal: controller.signal }) and calls controller.abort() to cancel; the SDK then sends notifications/cancelled and aborts the server handler through its signal.
In a cancellable server handler, poll extra.signal.aborted inside long loops/operations and stop work promptly (returning an error result) once cancellation is signalled.
Define tool input/output schemas as JSON Schema 2020-12: let McpServer with Zod convert them automatically, or supply JSON Schema directly when using the low-level Server.
Register tool and prompt input schemas with a Standard-Schema library (e.g. Zod v4) when defining the server under test.
Default to InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair() when unit- or integration-testing MCP server logic, and reserve stdio or Streamable-HTTP transports for end-to-end transport-level tests.
Use InMemoryTransport only for test/development in-process wiring; for production in-process connections use StreamableHTTPClientTransport against a local server URL.

Treat `protocol` as the mandatory foundation validator and respect validator dependency order (capabilities, ping, errors, security all depend on it); extend validation through the plugin model instead of ad-hoc checks.

Configure validation reproducibly through named profiles, a .mcp-validation.json config file, or the MCP_VALIDATION_CONFIG / MCP_VALIDATION_PROFILE environment variables (and tune validator parameters there) instead of ad-hoc one-off flags.

Beyond the CLI, validate containerized servers through the container runtime (e.g. podman/docker) and embed validation programmatically via the API (validate_server / validate_mcp_server_command) when automating.
Standardize the container-based validation invocation: run the tool via `uv run`, use podman with `-i --rm <image>:<version>`, and append the server's package_arguments after the image name.

Treat validation warnings as non-fatal but actionable: a server can pass with warnings, so triage recurring warning categories (container images not based on UBI, mcp-scan 'NoneType' failures, and JSON-RPC error-compliance issues) instead of ignoring them.

Diagnose common validation failures as a missing required package argument or an incorrect container image reference, and recognize that servers lacking a containerized distribution cannot be validated by the container-based flow.

When generating registry entries, extract environment-variable names verbatim from the server README (for example from `-e VARIABLE_NAME` Docker examples); never assume, invent, or standardize variable names.

Build the registry entry deterministically from the repository: clone it, derive metadata (uuid id, README-based description, GitHub repository fields), set version from the container image tag with is_latest true, model packages as a single docker entry, and store the result in registry.json conforming to the MCP registry OpenAPI schema.
